newsitem.title: USA: Mich. House won't mull $1 bln pension bond plan.
newsitem.headline: Mich. House won't mull $1 bln pension bond plan.

text.p: Michigan lawmakers will not adopt Treasurer Doug Roberts' proposed $1 billion school pension bond plan this session, a spokeswoman for the House Democratic caucus said Tuesday.
The pension bond plan to fully fund the teacher retirement system had been advanced by Michigan senators last week.

The package has been referred to the House appropriations and retirement committees and "at this point there is no plan for it to be moved out of committee before we recess," spokeswoman Andi Brancato said.
Roberts plan would require participating districts to drop any potential claims for past special education funding lapses and climb on board by August 15.
The deal in its present form is off, but elements of it may be offered at a later date, state budget department spokeswoman Maureen McNulty said.
The proposal would have taken advantage of current market conditions and those factors will change, McNulty noted.

Roberts had first proposed issuing up to $3.6 billion of taxable bonds for the plan, but revised the figure last month by raising actuarial valuations from 8 percent to 8.25 percent and pegging the unfunded liability as of June 30.
The proposal would have eliminated the state's unfunded liability and then offered employees the option of a pension plan or defined contribution.
A summary of the proposal noted that it could have cut pension costs $177 million per year and excess proceeds would then have been used to begin prefunding health benefits.

Roberts plan required districts to relinquish future claims against the state stemming from a legal challenge to Michigan's former special education funding formula. That lawsuit filed by 84 districts remains pending.
Michigan Supreme Court justices backed the school districts last month on the legal issue, but have not decided if they should be compensated for the claims.
The state budget office has estimated that Michigan could face a liability of from $500 million to $3.5 billion in retroactive and future claims from districts statewide.
Michigan lawmakers have not completed work on a road repair funding package or the transportation budget, but were hopeful of wrapping the session in the next few days.
